title: Match the .NET Fix
blurb: Knowing the risk is half of it — knowing the ASP.NET Core / .NET remediation is what gets it fixed. Match each vulnerability to how you actually address it in a .NET app.

levels.title: L1 · The core fixes
levels.prompt: Match each vulnerability to its .NET fix.

right.label: Parameterized queries — EF Core LINQ, FromSqlInterpolated, or Dapper parameters
Resource-based authorization — scope every query to the current user
Identity's PasswordHasher (PBKDF2), or bcrypt/Argon2 — slow and salted
User Secrets in dev; Azure Key Vault / managed identity in prod

levels.explain: SQL injection → parameterize (keep values out of the query text). IDOR → resource-based authorization (check ownership). Weak passwords → a slow salted hash. Leaked secrets → User Secrets / Key Vault, never in source.

failStates.title: Access control isn't a hashing problem
failStates.explain: IDOR is fixed by verifying the caller owns the resource (resource-based authorization), not by anything crypto-related.

levels.title: L2 · The rest
levels.prompt: Match each vulnerability to its .NET fix.

left.label: Verbose errors / dev page in prod

right.label: Razor auto-encoding — avoid @Html.Raw; encode any HTML you must build
Environment-based config — developer exception page only in Development; add security headers
Avoid BinaryFormatter / TypeNameHandling.All; use System.Text.Json with known types
Log security events (failed logins, denied access) and alert on them

levels.explain: XSS → let Razor encode output (avoid @Html.Raw). Verbose errors → only show the developer exception page in Development, add security headers. Unsafe deserialization → don't deserialize untrusted types; use System.Text.Json. No visibility → log and alert on security events.

failStates.title: Encoding doesn't fix deserialization
failStates.explain: Output encoding stops XSS. Unsafe deserialization is fixed by not binding untrusted input to arbitrary types — use System.Text.Json with known, expected types.
